provide some evidence that concrete evidence that they are becoming true. I hope I don't have to convince you that robot learning has made a lot of progress. And one of the key factors is that we have rediscovered teleoperation to be a really good way

to teach robot how to do really complex tasks like making laundries, clean bathrooms, or doing warehouse tasks. And they're really being deployed in the real world today, in factories, in laundromats, and they're starting to be usable,

but they're not mature yet. But we're seeing them in the world-- in the real world today. So before diving into the technical talk, I want to step back and ask a more fundamental question, why do we believe this whole data-driven robotics

direction will work at scale? After all of these hundreds of billions of dollars of investments in robotics right now, this underlying belief that we all think is going to work. So the answer really is largely based on analogy with the type of AI

we're using today. At this point, a large part of human knowledge is being captured by the internet. They get downloaded, cleaned, and absorbed by these large foundational models. And in other words, modern AI succeeds because we found a

scalable way to transfer our knowledge to these models through the internet. We, the robotics researchers, are essentially trying to apply the same idea to the physical world. Instead of semantic knowledge robots, it needs sensorimotor knowledge

or physical intelligence. So teleoperation really provides a mechanism to transfer this knowledge, by controlling robots while recording what the robot sees and what actions should be taken, we are building a direct mapping between the perception option,

or the input and output supervision for the robot's body. In a sense, teleoperation allows to transfer human physical intelligence to the robots. But despite the simplicity of this analogy, in reality, teleoperation creates a very, very tight

knowledge transfer bottleneck. And I argue there are two major factors to this bottleneck. The first one should be familiar to some, is the scalability problem. If you have ever tried teleoperation, it's very, very unintuitive. It takes a lot of

practice to get it right. More importantly, teleoperation only scales linearly. The amount of data we can collect grows only with the number of robots. Multiply the number of human teleoperation hours and compared to the internet scale data used

when a human deliberately acts sewer robots using interface like VR devices, and this creates a very indirect feedback loop that meddles with our natural behavior. As many forms of intelligence are difficult to deliberately demonstrate through teleoperation.

Think about subtle behaviors like needing a doll, or picking up a card by sliding to the edge of a table and picking it up, or when your hands are full, so you kick open a door instead of using a hand to open a door, right? So all of these motions,
